title: DynamoDB in depth
subtitle: Know what DynamoDB does with each request, and you can predict what it costs, when it throttles, and which guarantees you really get.

c.v: On Sunday, 20 September 2015, DynamoDB in AWS's US-East Region began returning errors at 2:19 a.m. Pacific time.
Inside DynamoDB, each table is split into

spread across storage servers. A server's list of partitions is its "membership". An internal metadata service keeps these lists. Servers check their list from time to time. If one cannot get it in time, it
(GSIs). Each GSI has its own partitions, so membership lists grew. A table with many partitions could see its share of these lists double or triple.
AWS later wrote: "We did not have detailed enough monitoring for this dimension (membership size)".

Then a short network blip made many servers ask for their lists at once. The metadata service slowed past the time limit. Servers that got no answer took themselves out of service and retried, which added more load. Even healthy servers started to fail their next renewals.
By 2:37 a.m., errors were far above anything seen in three years. They settled at about 55% of requests.

At 5:06 a.m., AWS paused requests to the metadata service. That cut the retries and took load off the service, so AWS could add capacity. By 7:10 a.m., errors were low enough for most customers to work normally. SQS, EC2 Auto Scaling, CloudWatch and the AWS Console were hit too.
A GSI looks like a small feature. Inside, it meant more partitions, more metadata and more work. That is why it helps to know what DynamoDB does with your table.

In DynamoDB, a cheap design is a correct design. Count the units each request uses, keep each partition under its limits, and read the fine print on every guarantee: indexes, transactions, TTL and global tables each have one.

c.v: Write the unit cost next to each access pattern: item size, read type, calls per second.
"What is the peak per partition key, not per table?"
1,000 write units a second (1,000 writes of up to 1 KB) is the ceiling.
Before you add a GSI, check its write capacity can match the table's. AWS says it should be equal or greater.
Avoid an LSI unless you need strong reads on another sort key. Ask if any partition key can grow past 10 GB.
Add a version attribute to every item that users edit, and use a condition on every write.
Treat TTL as cleanup, not as a timer. Filter expired items in reads.
Before a global table, list the items two Regions might change at once.

q.v: Your items are 6 KB each. How many read capacity units does one eventually consistent GetItem use?

options.v: 0.75, because 6 KB is three quarters of 8 KB.
1, because 6 KB rounds up to 8 KB, which is 2 units, and eventual reads cost half.
2, because eventual reads cost the same as strong reads.

why.v: Read sizes round up to the next 4 KB, so 6 KB counts as 8 KB, or 2 strongly consistent units. An eventually consistent read costs half of that.

q.v: A Query uses a FilterExpression that keeps 10 of the 1,000 items it reads. What do you pay for?

options.v: All 1,000 items read, because the filter runs after the read.
Nothing extra, because filters are free and reduce cost.

why.v: A filter is applied after the Query reads the items, so the read cost is the same with or without it.

q.v: A table's GSI is short of write capacity, while the table itself has plenty. What happens to writes on the table?

options.v: They succeed, and the index catches up later.
They can be throttled, because each table write must also fit in the index's write capacity.

why.v: The docs say a table write succeeds only if the table and all affected GSIs have enough write capacity. Otherwise the write is throttled.

q.v: Your service uses a global table in eventual (MREC) mode in two Regions. It checks a version number with a condition expression before each update. Two users update the same item at the same time, one in each Region. What can happen?

options.v: Both condition checks pass locally, and last writer wins drops one update.
DynamoDB rejects the second write with a conflict error.
The two updates are merged field by field.

why.v: In MREC, a condition is checked against the item in the local Region only. Conflicts across Regions are settled by last writer wins, so the version check does not protect you.

q.v: A Query returns zero items, but the response has a LastEvaluatedKey. What should your code do?

options.v: Stop. No items means the end of the results.
Send the next Query with ExclusiveStartKey set to that LastEvaluatedKey.
Retry the same Query, because the page failed.

why.v: The 1 MB limit applies before the filter, so a page can be empty and still not be the last. You are done only when LastEvaluatedKey is missing.
